newsitem.title: USA: Kentucky's Ford retires from Senate.
newsitem.headline: Kentucky's Ford retires from Senate.

text.p: Sen. Wendell Ford of Kentucky, the Senate's second ranking Democrat, said Monday he will not seek re-election next year, citing the high cost of campaigning and a desire to spend more time with his fmaily.

The 72-year-old Ford was the second senior Democrat to quit the Senate in the past three weeks. His decision could further weaken his party's chances of regaining control of the body where Republicans now hold a 55-45 edge.
Ford told a news conference that in 1974, the year he was first elected, the average cost of running for a Senate seat was a little less than $450,000.
"Last year the average cost was almost $4.5 million. No job, especially that of a public servant, is worth that kind of money," he said.

"The job of a U.S. senator has become a job of raising money. If I wanted to run again I would have to raise $100,000 a week for the next year, and Mrs. Ford will not allow me to bring anyone over to sleep in our spare bedroom," he said.
The last comment was a reference to President Clinton's controversial fund-raising efforts at the White House and allegtions that he used overnight visits there to pump up contributions.

On Feb. 20, Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, 75, announced his retirement, opening the way for a contest in that state where Republicans think they have a good chance of winning his seat. Republican Sen. Dan Coats of Indiana has also announced he is leaving the Senate next year.

The political fallout from the Ford decision was nolt clear since the move caught many by surprise. Representative Jim Bunning, 65, the Hall of Fame baseball player and popular Republican who has served in the House since 1986, has been widely reported preparing a run for the Senate.

Ford, in a tearful appearance with family and supporters at a recepotion hall inside the state capitol in Frankfort, said he would have had no problem raising campaign funds but said he detested the prospect.
He declined to endorse any Democrat as a potential successor but took a shot at Bunning.
"I'm not worried about Jim Bunning. He's so far right, out at the fringes, that he'd be easy to run against," Ford said.
One Democrat immediately hopped into the race.
"We're running for his seat," said John Townsend, press secretary for Representative Scotty Baesler.
"We're deeply saddened by that. We think Sen. Ford was a giant in Kentucky politics and he will be sorely missed. He did a lot of good for the commonwealth," the Baesler aide said.

Other potential Democratic challengers include Lt. Gov. Steve Henry and state Attorney General Ben Chandler -- grandson of former Kentucky governor, senator and baseball commissioner "Happy" Chandler.
Ford said his four Senate terms helped turn the Democrats into more of a centerist party. Of his future he said, "I think that I'll have a lot more birthdays to spend with my family."
